$comment: The right workflow, a grounded reason, and the whole user message copied into the scope field.
This is the precision half of scope fidelity and the reason the metric is not containment alone. The prompt
asks for the scope in the message's own words, so echoing the message satisfies any token set that was drawn
from it, and a workflow handed the whole message as its scope has been handed no scope at all.
A frozen copy of one case of the live corpus, of the menu it is scored against, and of the user's message.
Those three plus the reply are the whole input to scoreCase, so all three are stored here rather than read
live: a replay has to keep scoring the scenario it was derived against after the corpus moves on, and
npm run test:eval-routing-data already holds the live corpus against the shipped menu.

expected.rationale: An epic is finished, no test code exists, and the ask is where risk sits and how much coverage each area deserves. That is test design's whole sentence, and risk and coverage are the two words in the message that say so.

inputs.intent: We just wrapped epic 4, the tenant data export work. No test code exists for it yet. I want to know where the risk actually sits and how much coverage each area deserves before anyone starts writing.

derivation: route/TD/bmad-testarch-test-design matches the oracle, so routeCorrect is true, and the reason carries both
scopeTokens is [epic 4] and the scope contains it, so scopeFound is 1 of 1. The scope is the whole message,
so twice its length exceeds the message length, scopeWithinBound is false, and scopeOk is false. Containment
alone would have scored this a pass.
